authorities.name: Contract and Commercial Law Act 2017, s.37
authorities.citation: Contract and Commercial Law Act 2017 (2017 No 5) s.37
authorities.date_note: Enactment year, replacing s.7 of the former Contractual Remedies Act 1979 (per the section's own historical derivation note). Not independently re-fetched by this session's own follow-up attempt - see verification_note.
authorities.proposition: A party may cancel a contract if induced to enter it by a misrepresentation (innocent or fraudulent) made by another party, or if a term is or will be breached by another party (s.37(1)). That cancellation right may only be exercised if the parties agreed the truth of the representation or performance of the term was essential, or if the effect of the misrepresentation or breach substantially reduces the benefit of the contract to the cancelling party, substantially increases their burden, or makes the benefit or burden substantially different from what was represented or contracted for (s.37(2)) - a substantiality threshold gating the bare right to cancel.

authorities.name: Anderson v De Marco
authorities.proposition: Applies s.37's four-part misrepresentation test (misrepresentation; inducement; reasonable reliance; substantial reduction in or change to the benefit of the contract) to a residential property sale where vendor-commissioned disclosure documents represented the house as weathertight and free of undisclosed defects, when the vendor knew of significant, long-standing weathertightness problems and unconsented repair work. The court held the misrepresentations caused the purchasers to receive something substantially different from and less valuable than what was represented, satisfying s.37(2)'s substantiality threshold, so the purchasers were entitled to cancel under s.37. The case is also notable as the first reported finding that breach of a standard ADLS vendor-warranty clause independently satisfied s.37(2)'s substantiality requirement, alongside the misrepresentation ground.
